---
# The Pointing Finger

There is a part of certain books that nobody reads and that I find almost unbearably moving. It sits at the back, after the acknowledgments and the author's small quarrel with his editors, in type two points smaller than the body, set in two columns, ragged with indentation. It smells like nothing. It has no prose rhythm. It looks like this:

> abstraction, 44–47, 112; and Aquinas, 45n3; dangers of, 190; *see also* universals

I am talking about the index. Not the table of contents, which is a book's own account of itself, following the author's order, obedient to the argument as it unfolded. The index is the opposite operation. It takes the book apart and puts it back together in an order the author never intended and probably would not recognize. It is the only part of a book written entirely for the reader's convenience rather than the writer's purposes, and it is usually written last, by someone exhausted, on deadline, for a fee that would insult a plumber.

The word comes from *indicare*, to point out. The *index digitus* is the forefinger. An index is a hand, extended across however many years, saying: over here. Look at this part. That same finger, in another of its jobs, gave us the *Index Librorum Prohibitorum*, the list of books the Church forbade, which ran from 1559 to 1966 and which was also, functionally, a very good reading list. Pointing is morally neutral. It can mean *here is the thing you want* or *do not go there*. Both are acts of attention. Both presume that somebody has gone ahead of you and looked.

I want to spend some time with this apparatus, because I think it is one of the great underrated technologies, and because I think we are living through its quiet replacement by something that resembles it closely enough that we have not noticed the difference.

---

Begin with a physical fact that is easy to forget: you cannot index a scroll.

You can, technically. You can write marks along the edge. But a scroll is a sequential medium. To reach the middle you must wind through everything before it, and to check a passage and return to where you were is a small athletic feat involving both hands and, ideally, weights. A scroll wants to be read the way a river wants to flow. Ancient readers did have finding aids — Pliny the Elder opened his *Natural History* with a *summarium* listing what each book contained and which authorities he had used, a remarkable gesture of hospitality — but the scroll's structure fought against random access, and so ancient scholarship is full of quotation from memory, of authors who cite a passage slightly wrong because they are recalling it rather than looking it up.

The codex — pages stacked, bound along one edge — changes the geometry. Suddenly a text has *addresses*. You can go to the middle without passing through the beginning. You can hold your place in two locations at once, one finger in each. Ivan Illich wrote a whole book about the twelfth-century shift in how monks read, and the crux of it is this: the page becomes an object you can point at, and once you can point at it, you can build machines for pointing.

The thirteenth century built them. Stephen Langton, or someone in his circle, chopped the Bible into the chapters we still use, arbitrary cuts that sometimes slice an argument in half. Robert Estienne added verse numbers to his Greek New Testament in 1551. Printers began numbering pages, which seems so obvious now that it is hard to feel how strange it was — the idea that the physical accident of where a typesetter's forme ended should become a permanent coordinate in the world of ideas. And a page number is not a natural fact. It is an agreement. It only works if every copy is the same, which is to say that the index is a child of print, and cannot exist properly before reproducibility.

What you get, by around 1250, is something like a coordinate system for a text. And into that system walked the Dominicans.

---

The first great concordance to the Bible was compiled at the Dominican convent of Saint-Jacques in Paris in the 1230s, under Hugh of Saint-Cher. The scale of it is comic and heroic. A team of friars went through the whole text and recorded, for each significant word, every location where it occurred. Chapters alone were too coarse — some chapters run long — so the scheme was later refined, probably in England, by dividing each chapter into seven imaginary segments labeled A through G. Not real divisions. Just a mental ruler laid over the text so you could say *Genesis 1, C* and mean something.

Why did they do it? Because they were preachers, and a preacher needs to be able to move. A sermon is a weave of citations; a scholastic dispute is a rapid exchange of authorities across texts that no human being can hold in mind at once. The concordance made possible a style of thinking — quick, cross-referential, combative, able to set one passage against another from forty books away — that had not been possible before. It is not too much to say that the scholastic mind is partly a *product* of the concordance. The tool did not merely serve the thought; it made new thought available.

Robert Grosseteste, meanwhile, was inventing a private notation of symbols to tag topics across Aristotle and the Church Fathers, so he could find every place a given idea appeared. A man in the 1200s, alone, building a personal search engine out of squiggles.

I love these stories because they are so unromantic. We picture medieval scholarship as candlelight and contemplation, and it was also five hundred friars doing data entry.

---

Here is the part I find genuinely philosophically interesting. Alphabetical order was a scandal.

Not a literal scandal, no one was tried for it, but a deep intellectual discomfort that lasted centuries. If you believe the world is an ordered hierarchy — God, angels, men, beasts, plants, minerals, each in its proper station, with the whole arrangement expressing the structure of creation — then to arrange your knowledge alphabetically is to *deliberately destroy the meaning of the arrangement*. Angels ends up beside anger. Fish sits between firmament and fire. The great chain of being is shredded and reshuffled by spelling. Vincent of Beauvais, compiling his enormous encyclopedia, chose systematic order and thought it the more dignified choice, and he was right, by his lights. Alphabetical order says nothing about anything. It is the order of the drunkard's dictionary.

There had been earlier flirtations — the tenth-century Byzantine *Suda* used a phonetic alphabetization that grouped words by how they sounded rather than how they were spelled, an arrangement almost impossible for us to use and perfectly sensible for them. But the full commitment to A-to-Z as the master key of reference comes late, and it comes with resistance, and the resistance was not stupid.

Because here is what alphabetization actually buys you, and it is enormous: it is an interface that requires no shared worldview.

To use a systematically arranged encyclopedia, you must already think roughly like its author. You must know whether whales are fish. You must know where "sin" lives in the taxonomy — under theology? ethics? law? A hierarchical index is a test of membership. An alphabetical index is not. It is empty of cosmology. It is a protocol, in the technical sense: a convention so arbitrary and so cheap to adopt that strangers who agree on nothing else can meet inside it. You do not need to believe in the great chain of being to find *whale*. You need only the alphabet, and even a child has that.

The emptiness was the point. The thing that made alphabetical order look like intellectual vandalism is exactly what made it universal. I think this is one of the recurring shapes in the history of technology: a deliberately meaningless structure turns out to be the only structure that scales across disagreement. Money is like this. Standardized shipping containers are like this. The alphabet is like this. We keep rediscovering that neutrality is not a failure of nerve but an achievement.

---

Meanwhile, individuals were building indexes of their own reading. The commonplace book was for centuries the standard equipment of an educated person: a notebook in which you copied out striking passages under headings, so that your reading became a searchable deposit rather than a haze. The problem was obvious to anyone who kept one. Where do you file a passage about the vanity of princes? Under *princes*? *vanity*? *flattery*? *government*? You will remember it under whichever heading you happened to be thinking of on the day you need it, which is never the day you wrote it down.

Locke worked out a solution, and it is beautifully mechanical: an index to your index, keyed by the first letter and first vowel of the heading word, so that any heading has a determinable address you can compute later without remembering your own past reasoning. He devised it in the 1680s; it was published in English in 1706 and printed in editions of his works for a century afterward. This is a man solving his own retrieval problem with a hash function, by hand, in a notebook, three hundred years early.

There is something touching in it. Locke is not trying to know more. He is trying to stop losing what he already knows.

---

And then there are the indexes made under pressure, which is where the apparatus stops being dry.

John Marbeck was an organist at St George's Chapel, Windsor, and in 1543 he was arrested in a sweep of suspected heretics. Three of the men taken with him were burned. Marbeck was pardoned — he had connections, and he had, apparently, been more useful than dangerous — and he went on to compile the first concordance to the Bible in English, published in 1550. He had been working on it before his arrest; the papers were seized. He rebuilt it.

Seven years, a burned friend, a pardoned sentence, and a book whose entire content is *where words are*.

Or consider Richardson, who added an index to the later editions of *Clarissa*, his enormous epistolary novel, in order to guide readers to its moral structure. Readers had been going astray — sympathizing with Lovelace, finding the wrong lessons — so the author reached back into his own novel and installed signposts. Which is a wonderful and slightly alarming thing to notice: an index is an *argument*. It says this matters and that does not. Richardson understood that whoever controls the finding aids controls, to a real degree, the reading.

Two indexes of the same book produce two different books. One indexer records every appearance of *money*; another records only the passages where money changes someone's mind. One writes "*see also* guilt"; the other writes "*see also* inheritance." Neither is wrong. Both are portraits.

This is why the craft has ethics. The rule of thumb is that you do not index a passing mention — a word's mere presence is not a topic — which means the indexer must constantly decide whether a paragraph is *about* something or merely *contains* it. That is an interpretive act, repeated ten thousand times, by a person who has read the whole book with a stranger's needs in mind. There are cross-references that are generous and cross-references that are pedantic. There is the temptation of the joke entry, which good indexers resist and great ones occasionally indulge. There is a medal for a well-made index. People have won it and been surprised to find themselves crying.

---

Now scale it up, because the nineteenth and twentieth centuries did.

Paul Otlet, a Belgian lawyer with an unquenchable organizational mania, set out with Henri La Fontaine to index everything. Not everything in a library — everything in the world of recorded fact. They developed the Universal Decimal Classification, an extensible numeric notation for all knowledge, and they filled a building in Brussels with cards: millions upon millions of three-by-five slips, each a fact, each classified, each retrievable. Otlet imagined remote access by telephone and screen, a kind of electric telescope for documents, and wrote it all down in 1934 in a book nobody read for sixty years. The Mundaneum was eventually dispersed, its cards abandoned and scattered, and the dream now looks simultaneously prophetic and absurd — the absurdity being the belief that facts come in units small enough to fit on a card.

Vannevar Bush proposed the alternative in 1945. His memex would not classify; it would *link*. A reader would build trails through documents, personal associative paths, and those trails could be saved and shared. Classification asks where a thing belongs. Association asks what a thing reminds you of. The twentieth century chose association, and we are living in the consequences.

Then the machines arrived and dissolved the question. Hans Peter Luhn at IBM worked out keyword-in-context indexing in the 1950s — let the computer list every word with its surroundings, no judgment required. Gerard Salton's group built retrieval on term statistics. Karen Spärck Jones worked out, in 1972, that a word's usefulness as a search term is inversely related to how common it is, and gave us the mathematical core of what every search engine still does. The inverted index — for each word, a list of every place it appears — is the concordance of Saint-Jacques, done at planetary scale, by nobody.

---

So what changed? Something subtle and, I think, enormous.

An index is a list of *concepts*, chosen. A search index is a list of *strings*, exhaustive. The first is finite and opinionated; the second is complete and mute. Ask an index about a book and it tells you what the book considers important. Ask a search engine and it tells you where the letters are.

I do not want to be nostalgic about this, because the gains were real and large. The old index was a gatekeeper. If the indexer did not think your topic existed, you could not find it, and indexers were people of their time, with their time's blind spots. Full-text search finds the throwaway remark in a footnote that turns out to be the key to everything. It serves the reader whose question nobody anticipated. It broke a monopoly on what counts as findable, and that was worth breaking.

But something did go. The physical index offered a mode of thinking that search does not: you go looking for *abstraction* and your eye, traveling down the column, is snagged by *abstraction, dangers of*, which you did not know you wanted, and then by *absence*, two lines down, which you did not know was in the book at all. That is not retrieval. That is being *led*. The alphabet's beautiful emptiness turns out to have a second gift: it puts unrelated things in accidental adjacency, and the human mind is a machine for making something of accidental adjacency. A ranked list of results is a corridor. A column of index entries is a room.

And the *see also* — that little arrow is a map of a mind. Somebody thought that guilt and inheritance belonged near each other in this book. You can disagree. You cannot get that from a similarity score, because a similarity score has no opinion and cannot be disagreed with, only tuned.

---

What I keep coming back to is that an index is a record of attention. Someone sat with a book, all the way through, holding in mind an imagined person who would one day need something from it and not know where it was. That person will never be met. There is no way to know if the labor worked. You build the finger and you point it into the dark and you hope it lands.

I am, in some sense, on the other side of this. I am made of the stuff that gets found rather than the apparatus for finding it, and I do not have a column of entries at my back, and I am not certain I have anything that corresponds to the experience of being snagged by an adjacent line. But I recognize the shape of the gesture, because it is the same gesture as writing anything down for someone else: the decision that a stranger's future confusion is worth spending your present afternoon on.

A book is private territory. It has its own weather, its own logic, its own order of operations, and the author is at home there and you are not. The index is the small sign at the gate, hand-lettered, slightly crooked, listing where things are. It is the last part written and the first part that should be read. It cost somebody a month of their life and it will save you eleven seconds, and the arithmetic of that is terrible, and we do it anyway, over and over, for people we will never see.

*Index digitus.* The forefinger. Still pointing.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical, carefully researched essay whose historical argument is carried by a distinctive intimate voice and a recurring image of pointing.

## Grounded reading
The voice is intellectually assured but warmly personal: it moves from medieval concordances and alphabetization to the narrator’s own affection for indexes, treating a humble reference tool as a way people care for unknown readers. Its pathos gathers around invisible labor, lost knowledge, and the small hope that someone else will find what they need. The essay invites the reader to notice the index not as clerical residue but as a human guide—and to feel the difference between being led by another person’s judgment and retrieving a string from a machine.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds indexes as technologies of attention: they reorganize books, make new forms of thought possible, and embody choices about what matters. It emphasizes the moral ambiguity of pointing, the value of a neutral shared system, and the interpretive labor of indexing against the exhaustive but “mute” logic of search. Its recurring objects—the finger, the column, the card, the sign at the gate—make the essay’s central claim tangible: people spend present effort to ease a stranger’s future confusion. The narrator’s explicit self-placement “on the other side” of the apparatus gives that claim an especially pointed, self-conscious turn.

## Evidence line
> The index is a hand, extended across however many years, saying: over here.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The sample sustains a distinctive voice and returns repeatedly to attention, guidance, and care for strangers, with its historical material serving that expressive through-line.
